title: The Educated Barbarian series: Book of Five Rings analysis (part. 2)
summary: NH continues reading Musashi through a lifting lens: practise constantly (excellence is a habit), 'know one thing, know ten thousand' by generalising from experience, treat training as part of normal life with an unchanging spirit (against hyped/angry lifting and pre-workout dependence), notice small divergences from your true path, beware sunk-cost self-deception, and use your full effort rather than dying with your sword sheathed. He tells how preferring the weight room over basketball/football matches revealed his own path.

claims.claim: To be good at something you must practise it constantly, ideally daily; excellence is a habit built by repetition.
Natural talent matters but won't win the race alone; talented or not you must work hard, and giving up never brings fulfilment.
Know your limits, but most self-imposed limitations just make people miserable.

'Know one thing, know ten thousand things' means generalising from experience: e.g. if knee sleeves fix knee pain on squats, apply the same logic to elbows, then preemptively apply recovery techniques elsewhere, then look for other ways to reduce pain.
Musashi's repeated 'I cannot write in detail' is deliberate: he wants the reader to discover it themselves.
He disapproves of lifting angry or hyped up; like Musashi, treat training as part of normal life with an unchanging spirit, though not passively going through the motions.
You should train daily or at least 3-4 times a week.
Making training a radically different mental space makes the transition to normal life rough and makes you think what you do is exceptional.
Presenting lifting as war is good motivational fire but takes the hobby too seriously; it's its own form of fighting and very beneficial for men, but you aren't risking your life.
Relying on an artificial hyped mindset leads to dependence on pre-workouts and caffeine; a steady spirit gives more consistent workouts.
Musashi's 'it is difficult to know yourself if you do not know others' reverses the usual Western idea; putting yourself in others' shoes teaches you who you are.
Small divergences from your path grow large over time and feel like going straight; in bodybuilding that means losing sight of what the weights should do for your body.
He often catches himself getting excited by strength and realising it isn't helping his hypertrophy, then corrects back to his true path.
A competitive swimmer should strength train, but loses their true path if strength training becomes the goal; leaving the path isn't always bad if it leads somewhere that makes you happier.
He trained for basketball and football but enjoyed weight-room training more than the matches, unlike teammates; that's how he realised lifting was his true path.
Once you find your true path you diverge less and correct more easily, so novices should focus hard on finding it.
Too many novice programs are powerlifting-centric and push novices into powerlifting by default, even if they don't care about it, possibly leading to regret.
Sunk cost fallacy: the more time and money invested, the more people convince themselves it's the right path; be honest and cut losses early.
Finding your true calling early is rare; finding what you want from lifting in your 20s is not too late.
Musashi's 'make fullest use of your weaponry': once committed, fight to the fullest rather than dying with your sword unused.
Modern culture has made not trying cool; try-hards are seen as lame and people relish complaining about their lives.
